title: "Hazard a Guess"

Next month marks exactly fifty-five years since Dallin H. Oaks, then the newly inaugurated president of Brigham Young University, delivered a far-sighted address to the university community.[^1]

[^1]: Gambling, https://speeches.byu.edu/talks/dallin-h-oaks/gambling/, 18 August 1971

Of all the topics he could have chosen, across secular and religious, he selected one that felt foreign to his audience: gambling.

In that address, he warned of three distinct moral weaknesses that gambling introduces into a society.

First is the philosophy of "taking"—contrasting the teachings of Jesus Christ, which focus on giving and sacrifice, with a philosophy that focuses entirely on taking without producing anything of value in return.

Second is the destruction of character, as the quest to get "something for nothing" erodes virtues like hard work, industry, thrift, and service, replacing them with greed and idleness.

Third is the devastating harm to families and the vulnerable, noting that gambling drives participants to neglect their households or turn to crime, while state-sponsored lotteries disproportionately exploit the poor and elderly out of financial desperation.

Drawing on his background as a legal scholar, Oaks also detailed critical political and legal warning signs.

He rejected using gambling for public revenue, calling state-sanctioned vice a costly shortcut that damages the citizenry's moral fabric.

He emphasized the standard-setting role of the law, warning that legalization removes social stigma and signals to the public that the behavior is proper.

Finally, he noted its historical association with crime, acting as a catalyst for public corruption and racketeering.

![](images/20260718_080827.jpg)

This slow erosion of societal standards mirrors the pattern described by Alexander Pope in *An Essay on Man*:

> "Vice is a monster of so frightful mien, As, to be hated, needs but to be seen; Yet seen too oft, familiar with her face, We first endure, then pity, then embrace."

We see this exact cycle play out in modern culture.

Marijuana, once strictly an illicit drug, was first pushed into the mainstream under the banner of medicinal use.

Once that baseline was accepted, the push shifted seamlessly toward full recreational legalization.

The packaging and the names change, but the potency, the damage, and the underlying pattern remain exactly the same.

Likewise, in his 2007 book *China Road*, journalist Rob Gifford observed how a horse racing track in Wuhan circumvented China's strict anti-gambling laws by rebranding the entire enterprise as an intellectual exercise. He noted:[^2]

[^2]: China Road: A Journey into the Future of a Rising Power, Rob Gifford, 2007

> "You are not gambling, the legal fiction goes, you are merely 'wagering a guess' on which horse is the best, and you are rewarded for your intelligence if you guess correctly."

When direct paths are blocked, the promoters of vice simply rewrite the vocabulary to thrive in plain sight.

![](images/20220602_203518.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Tomorrow, on Sunday, 19 July 2026, the FIFA World Cup will conclude its 39-day rampage through the cities of Canada, the United States, and Mexico.

Like a long-forecasted tropical hurricane, its destructive forces have steadily gained momentum.

Yet, unlike a natural storm that absorbs its energy from warm ocean waters, the World Cup fuels itself on the vulnerabilities of people with gambling tendencies.

The resulting destruction is not measured in shattered buildings or property damage, but in the devastation of individuals, families, and a society that can least afford the devastating impact of gambling loss.

The warnings and predictions of Dallin H. Oaks have already come to pass.

However, extent of damage can be controlled.

The expansion of these destructive industries into our daily lives is neither based on natural law nor the commandments of established religions.

However, halting it requires us to change how we speak about it.

It is time to say things exactly as they are.

We must stop sugar-coating an industry designed to profit from human vulnerability.

We must reject the sanitized language of corporate PR and the legal fictions that turn a devastating vice into a harmless hobby.

It is not "gaming"—it is gambling. It is not "wagering a guess"—it is exploitation.

We must call it what it is: evil and destructive.

We use these strong words because this enterprise is not victim-less.

The casualties are real.

They are measured in ruined lives, broken families, and the quiet devastation of the people in our communities who can least afford the loss.

The first step toward action is absolute clarity. Only when we refuse to tolerate the sanitized lies can we begin to protect our homes, our society, and the generation coming next.
